sources.citation: Ravi Sankar S. Nair. 2013. Tribal Languages of Kerala. Language in India 13(7).
sources.note: Does not mention Kumbaran/Kumbharan at all (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: zero hits); no stress statement relevant to this variety.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2006. Change Request 2006-008: create [wkb] Kumbaran (submitted by Barb Waugh, SIL, 2006-05-22; adopted 2007-07-18). 4 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or phonology. States only that Kumbaran speakers 'call their language Telugu' but the NLCI Wayanad survey found it 'only 48% lex. similar to Telugu', and cites Iyer-type sources that the Kumbaran 'speak their own caste dialect that is related to Telugu but is a mixture of other Dravidian languages'. Sources listed: Mathew et al. 2004 (unpublished NLCI survey), IJFM 14(3) 1997, KRPCDS potters survey, an ethnographic pottery report.

sources.citation: Lalithambika, K. [c. 2000-01]. Techno-socio-economic survey on the living and working conditions of the traditional potter communities of Kerala. KRPLLD report, Centre for Development Studies, Thiruvananthapuram.
sources.note: Nothing on language beyond community names (Kumbaran found in Palakkad, Trissur, Kozhikode, Wynad; Tulu-speaking Kulalas in Kasaragod). No linguistic description.

sources.citation: 'The Kumbaran of India'. International Journal of Frontier Missions 14(3), Jul-Sep 1997, 1 p.
sources.note: Nothing. Missions profile: 'Telugu is the common caste language among all potters in addition to the language of the state in which they reside.'

sources.citation: Iyer, L. K. Ananthakrishna. 1912. The Cochin Tribes and Castes, Vol. II, chap. XIV 'Kumbaran'. Madras: Higginbotham & Co. (archive.org DLI scan;ernet.dli.2015.39815, scanned text)
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic chapter: 'Kumbarans, otherwise called in Telugu Kummaravadu, are a Telugu caste of potters found in small communities in the Trichur and Mukundapuram taluks of the State. They are mostly immigrants from the Tamil districts of Trichinopoly and Madura.' No language data; the 13 'stress'/'accent' hits in the full volume are all non-linguistic (mistress, distress, accentuated).
